title: The Night Tuskegee's Third Brick Kiln Fell
dek: In Tuskegee's early years, three kilns of student-made bricks failed, the money ran out, and Booker T. Washington pawned a watch to try a fourth.

story.company: Tuskegee Normal School (later Tuskegee Institute and Tuskegee University)
story.event: Three failed brick kilns and the pawned watch that paid for a fourth
story.summary: In Tuskegee's early years Booker T. Washington set students to make bricks for the school's own buildings; by his 1901 account three kilns failed, the last collapsing near the end of a week's burning, and most teachers advised giving up. He pawned a watch in Montgomery for fifteen dollars and a fourth kiln succeeded; in an 1899 telling the money paid a skilled man to burn the bricks and teach the students. By 1884 the students were making bricks for Alabama Hall, and the brickyard went on to sell to the town.
paragraphs: Burning a kiln of bricks took about a week. Towards the end of one such week in Tuskegee's early years, Booker T. Washington expected several thousand good bricks within hours. In the middle of the night, he later wrote, the kiln fell. "For the third time we had failed."

The school had opened on 4 July 1881 in a leaky building owned by a church, and soon moved to an abandoned former cotton plantation outside the town. From the start Washington wanted students to put up their own buildings. Many advised against it; he expected mistakes and argued that they would teach. In April 1883 a visitor from Hampton Institute reported that Washington planned to build with brick from the farm's clay. There was no brickyard in town, and local people wanted bricks too. What he had, in his phrase, was the task of making "bricks with no money and no experience."

It went badly. Students, many from plantation cabins, disliked standing knee-deep in the mud-pit, and more than one left the school. Good clay had to be hunted for. The first kiln, of about 25,000 bricks, was badly built and badly burned; the second failed too, and fewer students would help. Teachers trained in Hampton's workshops volunteered for the third. When it collapsed, Washington had no money left, and most of the teachers advised giving up.

He took a watch to a pawnshop in Montgomery, raised fifteen dollars, and began a fourth kiln. It worked. He never redeemed the watch. In an account published in 1899 he told it a little differently: none of them had known how to burn bricks, and the pawn money paid a skilled man to burn them and teach the students. By spring 1884 he was telling Northern audiences that his young men had made two kilns of bricks for a new hall. White neighbours who had had nothing to do with the school began buying them, and within two decades the brickyard was turning out more than a million bricks a year, by Washington's counts.

quote.text: By well-known road, though travelled many times before, Without a guide to venture, opens peril's door. How then an unknown path thou ne'er hast followed yet? Go not alone, without a guide;--act not in fret.
quote.locator: Book I, section X ("Patience and Perseverance under a Teacher"), couplets 11-12
quote.source_title: The Mesnevi, tr. Sir James W. Redhouse, Project Gutenberg eBook #61724
quote.connection: Washington admitted he had thought brickmaking simple. The kilns came closest to working when Hampton-trained teachers joined in, and in one of his tellings the fourth worked because the pawn money bought a skilled burner who taught them. Rumi, writing of a spiritual teacher, says the same of any unknown road.

reflection: Washington's two tellings disagree about how the fourth kiln was won. In one, it was persistence and a pawned watch. In the other, the watch bought a skilled man's time and his teaching. The second is less dramatic, and perhaps more useful.

When something you are building keeps failing, the instinct is often to try once more, harder, and alone. Sometimes the better move is to find the one person who has done this particular thing before and ask for an hour of their attention. Asking is not a failure of nerve. It may be the cheapest attempt you make.
invitation: Think of one task that has failed on you more than once. Before trying it again, write down the name of someone who has done it well, and send them one specific question this week.

research_notes: Every account of the failed kilns traces back to Washington himself, and his two tellings differ. Up from Slavery (1901) says three kilns failed (the first badly built and burned, the second for unknown reasons, the third collapsing near the end of its week), that the pawned watch raised fifteen dollars, and that the fourth attempt succeeded. Washington's earlier account, quoted by M. B. Thrasher in Popular Science Monthly (September 1899), mentions no count of failures: they could make bricks but could not burn them, and the pawned gold watch paid a skilled man to burn them and teach the students. The story gives both and says which is which. Scott and Stowe (1916) confirm only 'a series of failures'. Dates: Washington gives none for the kilns. The Story of My Life and Work (1900) quotes J. F. B. Marshall's report of an April 1883 visit, when Washington was still planning to build with the farm's clay, and Washington's address on a Northern tour in spring 1884 saying the young men 'have already made two kilns of bricks'; the episode therefore falls in 1883 or early 1884, and the story says 'in Tuskegee's early years' with those two dated markers. Output figures differ: Up from Slavery (1901) says 1,200,000 bricks 'last season'; The Story of My Life and Work (1900) says 1,500,000 'last year alone'. The story uses the conservative 'more than a million bricks a year, by Washington's counts'. The farm's price and loan also differ (Up from Slavery: $500 with a $250 loan; NPS: $200 down; The Story of My Life and Work: a $500 loan) and are not used. Funding is recorded as mixed: the state paid teachers' salaries (a $2,000 appropriation, raised to $3,000 in 1883) while buildings depended on donations and student labour. The quoted Up from Slavery is used only as a story source, not for the quote. The Rumi passage is about a spiritual teacher (pir) and is applied by analogy.
